sources.description: A historical study written in 1949 and published in 1981. Quigley traces elite networks through education, publishing, imperial governance and foreign policy. His appendix labels the membership roster tentative, with possible errors and explicitly bracketed conjectures. The archive distinguishes reported roles from his inferred affiliations. The PDF remains a local research document and is not redistributed by this site.
sources.coverage: All 13 chapters represented by selected records; the tentative appendix roster is indexed. Not every name, date, footnote, or passing reference has been extracted.

sources.title: The State, the Deep State, and the Wall Street Overworld
sources.author: Peter Dale Scott
sources.description: An Asia-Pacific Journal / Japan Focus article examining the interplay of security institutions, financial elites and international covert operations. Causal arguments and quoted interpretations are attributed to Scott or their named authors; the notes include denials and evidentiary qualifications. The PDF header gives March 3, the recommended citation March 10, and the revision March 13, 2014.
sources.coverage: Article and all endnotes reviewed. Selective extraction of dated events, institutions and people; passing names are not exhaustive.

evidenceIssues.description: Publication header and recommended citation disagree (March 3 versus March 10); explicit update March 13, 2014.
Scott notes establishment writers describe Copeland memoirs as unreliable; claims from Copeland remain attributed.
Nixon briefcase donation story is disputed by Kolb, and Baer gives 1968 rather than 1972; not included as a factual dated event.
Safari Club resort and intelligence alliance are separate entities; Scott presents both official-policy origin and later circumvention interpretations.
Notes 103 and 105 explicitly state no published evidence Copeland was involved in Safari Club covert operations; no membership edge created.
Scott’s oil-boycott interpretation is denied by Exxon corporate history in note 48.
The article’s parenthetical company labels conflate Standard Oil of New York/Socony and California. A collective oil-cartel record avoids reproducing the naming error.
Ownership and job descriptions are historical statements as of the 2014 article, not claims about current roles.

sources.title: The Yankee and Cowboy War
sources.author: Carl Oglesby
sources.subtitle: Conspiracies from Dallas to Watergate
sources.description: Oglesby interprets Dallas, Watergate and the Hughes business struggle through competing elite factions. Yankee and Cowboy are his analytical labels, not verified formal organizations. Alternative assassination, covert-operation and sabotage theories remain source-attributed; denials and official accounts are preserved.
sources.coverage: Selected records across the narrative, 1977 preface and appendix, with notes and index used as finding aids. The scan contains OCR errors; names and dates are normalized cautiously. This is an attributed digest, not an exhaustive extraction of every reference.

events.name: Secret banking conference at Jekyll Island
events.description: Scott presents the secret 1910 bankers’ conference as an antecedent of the Federal Reserve and an illustration of enduring financial influence over government. Nelson Aldrich and Paul Warburg figure in his account, while recollections by Warburg and B. C. Forbes provide the narrative of secrecy surrounding the meeting.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Roosevelt observation about financial power
events.description: Scott invokes a 1933 remark by Franklin Roosevelt to Edward House to support his argument that financial influence long preceded the CIA. Roosevelt’s reported observation placed powerful financial interests above the government from the era of Andrew Jackson onward. Scott treats the statement as an interpretive starting point rather than a demonstrated institutional history.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Dulles negotiates with Karl Wolff
events.description: Scott argues that Allen Dulles’s 1945 negotiations with SS General Karl Wolff over German forces in Italy exemplified private judgment overriding Washington’s instructions. He connects the negotiations to Roosevelt’s agreement with Stalin on unconditional surrender and presents this breach as one contributing factor in the emerging Cold War.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Dulles convenes CIA planning advisers
events.description: In Scott’s account, Director of Central Intelligence Hoyt Vandenberg recruited Allen Dulles in 1946 to help design the agency that became the CIA. Dulles, then practicing at Sullivan and Cromwell, assembled six advisers, all but one from Wall Street banking or law. Scott emphasizes their later movement into government.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: CIA-backed funding for Italian election
events.description: Scott describes intervention in Italy’s 1948 election as an early CIA covert operation financed with more than $10 million in captured Axis funds. Fundraising began in New York’s wealthy Brook Club, but Allen Dulles persuaded Washington to authorize an intelligence operation rather than rely solely on a private fundraising campaign.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: American Committee for a United Europe established
events.description: Scott says Allen Dulles established the American Committee for a United Europe in early summer 1948, before formally joining the CIA. He links the committee’s support for European integration to an operation that became exceptionally large within the CIA’s Western European activity by the early 1950s.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Marshall Plan funds support political warfare
events.description: Scott argues that the Marshall Plan provided reconstruction assistance and a funding channel for covert political warfare. Drawing on Tim Weiner, he says Allen Dulles, George Kennan and James Forrestal helped devise a secret provision allowing the CIA to divert millions of dollars. Frank Wisner then supervised an enlarged covert program.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Allen Dulles formally joins CIA
events.description: Scott dates Allen Dulles’s formal entry into the CIA to November 1950 and contrasts it with substantial earlier involvement in intelligence-related activity. His examples include agency planning, European anti-Soviet propaganda, the American Committee for a United Europe and election funding. Scott argues that formal office did not define the boundaries of Dulles’s influence.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Oil majors boycott Iranian exports
events.description: Scott describes a May 1951 boycott of Iranian oil exports following Mossadeq’s nationalization of Anglo-Iranian Oil Company interests. He argues that the other oil majors backed the boycott because nationalization threatened their own position. His notes also record a contrary account: Exxon’s corporate history denies a coordinated conspiracy to boycott Iranian oil.

events.name: Helliwell helps establish Sea Supply
events.description: Scott describes Sea Supply as a CIA-controlled company that provided weapons and equipment to forces in Southeast Asia. An endnote cites a Wall Street Journal account saying Paul Helliwell helped establish and run it in 1951. Scott links the supply infrastructure to CIA-supported armies and drug trafficking in the region.

Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Truman administration pursues oil-cartel case
events.description: Scott says Truman’s Justice Department sought in 1952 to challenge agreements through which major oil companies controlled global distribution. When ordered to provide documents, Exxon lawyer Arthur Dean of Sullivan and Cromwell refused on national-security grounds. Scott presents the response as an example of corporate policy priorities being defended against public regulation.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Royal Navy intercepts Iranian-oil tanker
events.description: Scott’s endnote describes Mossadeq trying to break the oil embargo in July 1952 by arranging a sale to a small Italian company. The British Royal Navy intercepted the tanker Rose Mary and redirected it to Aden. Scott says news of the interception discouraged other tankers from attempting to reach Abadan.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: CIA officials begin Iran-operation planning
events.description: Scott dates the start of CIA planning for intervention in Iran to November 1952, connecting it to existing efforts by MI6 and oil companies. He distinguishes this planning phase from Eisenhower’s final approval in July 1953. That gap is central to his argument that intelligence joined a campaign already under way.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Copeland returns to Cairo with Booz Allen mission
events.description: In March 1953 Miles Copeland returned to Cairo after leaving the CIA for Booz Allen. Scott quotes Copeland’s characterization of the assignment as effectively a joint intelligence and consulting mission. Besides economic management advice, Copeland advised Nasser about establishing an intelligence service and became an important channel to the US government.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Eisenhower approves TP/AJAX
events.description: Scott dates Eisenhower’s final approval of TP/AJAX to July 22, 1953. He argues that the CIA and MI6 operation against Mossadeq joined a campaign the oil companies had begun two years earlier. The resulting arrangement strengthened American oil majors by giving them a share of production previously associated with Anglo-Iranian.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Oil antitrust criminal case replaced by civil action
events.description: Scott argues that Eisenhower’s administration weakened the oil-cartel antitrust case by replacing criminal charges with a civil action and shifting responsibility toward the State Department. He stresses the overlap between Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and Sullivan and Cromwell, the firm defending the oil companies and his former workplace.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Booz Allen begins overseas assignments
events.description: Scott says Booz Allen began overseas assignments in 1953 involving Philippine land registration, Egyptian customs and textiles, and Iran’s national oil company. He argues that all three overlapped CIA operations, making the consulting firm an early example of the relationship between private contractors and intelligence work that he later describes as a revolving door.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: British authorization channel arranged for U-2 flights
events.description: Scott says Allen Dulles arranged in 1957 for some U-2 flights over the Soviet Union to be authorized by British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan through MI6. He portrays this as a way around Eisenhower’s reluctance to approve more than occasional flights and as another instance of intelligence officials circumventing a political superior’s constraints.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: CIA considers Moss for political action
events.description: Scott says the CIA decided in November 1962 to use Edward K. Moss for the Political Action Group of its Covert Action staff while planning against Castro. He contrasts that decision with earlier FBI warnings about Moss’s associates, using the combination to examine relationships between intelligence work and allegedly criminal networks.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: CIA political action project against Indonesian PKI
events.description: Scott describes a November 1964 US decision to have the CIA covertly support people and organizations willing to obstruct Indonesia’s Communist Party. He connects the policy to identifying opponents of Sukarno and potential leaders of a successor regime. The endnote identifies a CIA Political Action Project dated November 19.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Lockheed shifts Indonesian intermediary contract
events.description: Scott says Lockheed shifted its Indonesian payments in May 1965 to a new contract with a company established by longtime agent August Munir Dasaad, despite objections from company counsel. He highlights Dasaad’s movement toward Suharto’s circle through General Alamsjah and links the payment channel to Indonesia’s approaching political transition.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Rockwell aircraft agreement with Indonesian Army
events.description: Scott describes a July 1965 Rockwell-Standard agreement to deliver two hundred Aero-Commander light aircraft to Indonesia’s army within the following two months. He identifies commission agent Bob Hasan as a Suharto associate and eventual business partner, emphasizing that the aircraft went to the army rather than the air force.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Indonesian September coup drama
events.description: Scott focuses on the Diponegoro division’s presence on both sides of Indonesia’s September 1965 coup drama and on business networks around Suharto. He connects aircraft procurement, shipping companies and oil-company payments to the political transition, arguing that military finance deserves attention alongside the immediate sequence of the coup attempt and suppression.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Copeland establishes close Khashoggi contact
events.description: Scott dates Miles Copeland’s close contact with Adnan Khashoggi to 1966, while Copeland was on leave from Booz Allen. The partnership joined political access and arms-sale commissions. Copeland later described a private intelligence enterprise built around client companies, but Scott expressly notes that several writers have challenged the reliability of his memoirs.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Khashoggi supplies plane for Nixon Middle East tour
events.description: Scott cites Anthony Summers’s account that Khashoggi provided Nixon a plane for a Middle East tour after the 1967 Six-Day War. Khashoggi then opened an account through a proxy at Bebe Rebozo’s Florida bank. Scott presents these favors and banking contacts as a means of cultivating access to a potential president.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Lockheed commissions paid to Khashoggi
events.description: Scott cites Lockheed’s acknowledgment of $106 million in commissions to Adnan Khashoggi between 1970 and 1975. The amount, more than ten times the payments to its next major intermediary, Yoshio Kodama, illustrates the scale of Saudi arms sales and helps explain Khashoggi’s ability to finance political access and regional proposals.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Colby dismisses James Angleton
events.description: Scott discusses William Colby’s 1974 dismissal of counterintelligence chief James Angleton through Joseph Trento’s account of the CIA’s internal conflicts. Trento portrays the dismissal and Watergate as catalysts for Richard Helms and Theodore Shackley to cooperate with outside partners. Scott uses this interpretation to explain claims of increasingly privatized intelligence work.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Safari Club intelligence alliance established
events.description: Scott describes the 1976 Safari Club alliance of French, Egyptian, Saudi, Moroccan and Iranian intelligence services as a response to American intelligence restrictions. He quotes Turki bin Faisal on that purpose, but also presents Mahmood Mamdani’s account of an alliance established with Henry Kissinger’s blessing. These accounts complicate a wholly unauthorized origin story.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Bush takes post-CIA banking position
events.description: Scott quotes Kevin Phillips on George H. W. Bush’s move from the CIA in January 1977 to chairmanship of the executive committee of First International Bancshares and its British subsidiary. He connects the banking role to a wider discussion of Safari Club financing, while the claims about BCCI dealings remain attributed to the cited authors.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Sadat visits Jerusalem
events.description: Scott cites Mahmood Mamdani’s account that the Safari Club helped prepare Anwar al-Sadat’s November 1977 visit to Jerusalem. A proposed meeting traveled from Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin to Sadat through the club’s Moroccan representative. Scott treats this diplomatic success as evidence that the alliance initially operated within recognizable American strategic objectives.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Israeli and Sudanese figures meet at Kenyan resort
events.description: Scott cites Theodore Draper on a May 1982 meeting at Khashoggi’s Kenyan safari resort involving Sudanese President Nimeiri, Israeli Defense Minister Sharon, and intermediaries Yaacov Nimrodi, Al Schwimmer and David Kimche. He uses the meeting to show that the Israelis involved in the later Iran initiative already knew Khashoggi and his regional network.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Khashoggi submits Middle East Peace Fund proposal
events.description: Scott describes Khashoggi, Copeland and Kolb developing a Middle East aid proposal modeled on the Marshall Plan. A note dates a confidential paper to Reagan to May 17, 1983 and describes up to $300 billion in regional aid. Scott argues that the proposal demonstrates Khashoggi’s usefulness as an intermediary between Israel, Arab governments and Washington.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Hamburg meeting prepares Iran arms initiative
events.description: Scott compares accounts of an April 1985 Hamburg meeting that brought Khashoggi and Iranian dealer Manucher Ghorbanifar together with Israeli and American-connected intermediaries. Draper emphasizes the start of the Iran arms affair; Copeland and Kolb describe a broader strategic opening. Scott supplements the memoir accounts with congressional findings about arms financing through BCCI.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: BCCI collapses amid investigations
events.description: Scott describes BCCI’s 1991 collapse as the end of a bank whose intelligence connections and warning signs had long been known to American authorities. He cites Richard Kerr’s acknowledgment that the CIA used BCCI for intelligence gathering and an inquiry alleging years of inaction by several agencies despite numerous reports of illegal activity.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Kerry–Brown BCCI report published
events.description: Scott repeatedly uses the December 1992 Kerry–Brown Senate report to distinguish official findings from memoir accounts about BCCI. The report identifies Khashoggi and Ghorbanifar as central Iran-Contra intermediaries, describes loan financing through the bank, and supplies evidence about BCCI’s intelligence connections. It anchors several of Scott’s broader claims about private financial networks.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Booz consulting firm splits
events.description: Scott describes the consulting firm’s 2008 separation into government-focused Booz Allen Hamilton and commercial and international Booz and Company. He places the corporate change inside his account of intelligence contracting, noting Carlyle’s majority ownership of Booz Allen and career exchanges between the contractor and senior intelligence offices. These descriptions concern the article’s historical period.

history.note: Added from scott; interpretation and date precision remain attributed.
Expanded source narrative and timeline context.

events.name: Federal Reserve supports bank rescue
events.description: Scott presents the 2008 financial rescue as evidence of the Federal Reserve and major banks’ political influence across party lines. He emphasizes support from successive Republican and Democratic administrations for public money to rescue large banks. The episode extends his historical argument from the Federal Reserve’s origins to contemporary financial power.
